title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: When Pierre and his wife entered the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual states in which she needed the mental effort of playing patience. So—though out of habit she greeted him with the words she always used when Pierre or her son returned: "High time, my dear! We've been waiting and waiting. Thank heaven you're here!"—and when she received her presents said the same words she always said: "It's not the gift that counts, my dear... thank you for thinking of an old woman like me..."—it was clear that Pierre's arrival annoyed her at that moment because it distracted her from her unfinished game.

She finished the game and only then examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sevres teacup with shepherdesses painted on it and a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the late count's portrait on the lid, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had been wanting this for a long time, but now she didn't feel like crying and so she looked at the portrait indifferently and focused instead on the card box.

"Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all you've brought yourself back—this has been absolutely ridiculous. You really must scold your wife! What are we to do with her? Without you she's like a madwoman! She doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she said with her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeevna," she added to her companion, "see what a fine card box my son has brought us!"
Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had much to talk about that they couldn't discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind that if they had started talking about anything in front of her, they would have had to answer her irrelevant questions and repeat things she'd already been told. They would have had to explain that so-and-so was dead, or so-and-so was married, which she would forget again the next time—yet they sat at tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the old countess's questions that were of no interest to anyone, whether Prince Vasili had grown old, whether Countess Mary Alexeyevna had sent her love and still remembered them, and other matters the countess herself cared nothing about.

The talk went on through tea, of the kind that interests nobody and can never be avoided. All the grown-ups were gathered around the round tea table, where Sonya presided over the samovar. The children had had their tea with their tutors and governesses, and their voices carried in from the next room. Everyone had a usual place. Nicholas took his tea at a little table beside the stove. On the armchair next to him lay Milka, the old gray borzoi, daughter of the first Milka. Her face was quite gray now and her large black eyes seemed to stand out more than ever. Denisov, his curls, mustache and whiskers half gray, sat next to Countess Mary with his general’s tunic unbuttoned. Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He spoke of things he knew the old lady could follow and would like to hear. He brought news of society and of her own circle, once a real, living, distinct company of people, most of them now scattered over the world and gathering, like her, the last ears of the harvests they had sown in younger days. Yet to the old countess these contemporaries of hers were the only society that was serious or real. Natasha could tell by Pierre’s animation that his visit had been interesting and he had plenty to say, but daren’t say it in front of the old countess. Denisov, outside the family, missed the reason for his caution. As a discontented man himself he took a keen interest in what was happening in Petersburg and kept pressing Pierre about the Semyonovsky regiment, then Arakcheyev, then the Bible Society. Once or twice Pierre got carried away and began to tell them, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan and Countess Mary Alexeyevna.
"And all this nonsense about Gossner and Tatawinova?" Denisov asked. "Is that weally still going on?"
"Going on?" Pierre exclaimed. "Worse than ever! The Bible Society is practically running the government!"
"What's that, my dear?" asked the countess, who had finished her tea and was clearly looking for a reason to be cross after her meal. "What are you saying about the government? I don't understand."

"Well, you know, Mama," Nicholas put in, knowing how to translate things into his mother's language, "Prince Alexander Golitsyn has founded a society, and as a result he has a great deal of influence, they say."
"Arakcheyev and Golitsyn," Pierre said incautiously, "are practically the whole government! And what a government! They see treason everywhere and are frightened of everything."

"Well, and what's wrong with Prince Alexander? He's a most estimable man. I used to see him at Maria Antonovna's," said the countess in an offended tone; and still more offended that everyone remained silent, she went on: "Nowadays everyone finds fault with everything. A Bible society—well, what harm is there in that?" and she got up—everyone rising with her—and with a stern expression sailed back to her table in the sitting room.
The gloomy silence that followed was broken by the sounds of children's voices and laughter from the next room. Clearly some exciting game was going on in there.
"Finished, finished!" little Natasha's gleeful shout rose above them all.
Pierre exchanged glances with Countess Mary and Nicholas (he never lost sight of Natasha) and smiled happily.
"That's delightful music!" he said.
"It means Anna Makarovna has finished her stocking," said Countess Mary.

"Oh, I'll go and see," said Pierre, jumping up. "You know," he added, stopping at the door, "why I'm especially fond of that music? It's always the first thing that tells me all is well. Coming home today, the nearer I got to the house the more anxious I grew. When I came into the front hall and heard Andrusha laughing his head off upstairs, I knew everything was fine."
"I know! I know that feeling," said Nicholas. "But I can't go in there—those stockings are meant to be a surprise for me."
Pierre went in to the children, and the shouting and laughter grew even louder.

"Come on, Anna Makarovna," Pierre's voice could be heard saying, "come here into the middle of the room. At the word of command: 'One, two,' and when I say 'three'... You stand here, and you go in my arms—now then! One, two!..." said Pierre, and silence followed. "Three!" And an ecstatic roar of children's voices filled the room.

This meant two stockings, which Anna Makarovna used to knit simultaneously on the same needles by a secret technique known only to her, and which she would always triumphantly pull—one from inside the other—in the children's presence when they were finished.
